text: # USCIS EB-1A policy notes (starter corpus) This file is a concise paraphrase for local development, not a substitute for the live Policy Manual. The official source is [6 USCIS-PM F.2, Extraordinary Ability](https://www.uscis.gov/policy-manual/volume-6-part-f-chapter-2). USCIS's October 2, 2024 clarification is [PA-2024-24](https://www.uscis.gov/sites/default/files/document/policy-manual-updates/20241002-ExtraordinaryAbility.pdf). For production use, refresh this corpus from the current USCIS source and retain source version/date metadata. ## Overall framework The E11 extraordinary ability classification concerns people in the sciences, arts, education, business, or athletics. The evidentiary review has two stages. First, the petitioner must show a major internationally recognized award or documentation satisfying at least three of the ten regulatory criteria (or qualifying comparable evidence where the criteria do not readily apply). USCIS then evaluates the petition in its entirety in a final merits determination, considering whether the person has sustained national or international acclaim, recognized achievements, and is among the small percentage at the top of the field. Three checkmarks alone do not establish eligibility. Evidence quality, context, and significance matter. ## Criterion 1 — Awards Evidence may concern nationally or internationally recognized prizes or awards for excellence in the field. Relevant questions include the award's scope, selection process, reputation, and whether it recognizes excellence in the person's field. USCIS clarified that qualifying team awards may be considered and that past awards are not excluded merely because they are not recent. [6 USCIS-PM F.2(B)(1); PA-2024-24] ## Criterion 2 — Membership The association's membership must require outstanding achievements, as judged by recognized national or international experts in the relevant field. Ordinary membership, payment of dues, or experience-based admission alone may be insufficient. USCIS clarified that past memberships can be considered. [6 USCIS-PM F.2(B)(1); PA-2024-24] ## Criterion 3 — Published material about the person The material must be about the person and relate to their work in the field; the source must qualify as a professional publication, major trade publication, or other major media. Capture title, author, date, outlet, and circulation or audience information where available. USCIS clarified that the material need not independently demonstrate the value of the person's work to satisfy the plain criterion. [6 USCIS-PM F.2(B)(1); PA-2024-24] ## Criterion 4 — Judging

Invitations alone may not establish completed participation; document the event, role, date, and work reviewed. [6 USCIS-PM F.2(B)(1)] ## Criterion 5 — Original contributions of major significance The contribution should be original and of major significance to the field, not merely useful to one employer or described as innovative. Evidence may explain adoption, influence, citations, implementation, independent recognition, or field-level impact, supported by documentation. [6 USCIS-PM F.2(B)(1)] ## Criterion 6 — Scholarly authorship Evidence concerns authorship of scholarly articles in the field in professional or major trade publications or other major media. Identify the work, authorship, publication venue, date, and why the venue and work qualify as scholarly. [6 USCIS-PM F.2(B)(1)] ## Criterion 7 — Artistic exhibitions or showcases The criterion expressly concerns display of the person's work at artistic exhibitions or showcases. USCIS clarified that non-artistic exhibitions should only be considered through a properly supported comparable-evidence argument, not automatically as this criterion. [6 USCIS-PM F.2(B)(1); PA-2024-24] ## Criterion 8 — Leading or critical role The role must be for an organization or establishment with a distinguished reputation. For a leading role, evidence should establish leadership within the organization. For a critical role, evidence should show contributions of significant importance to the outcome of the organization's activities. The role can be for a distinguished department or division, not only the entire organization. [6 USCIS-PM F.2(B)(1); PA-2022-12] ## Criterion 9 — High salary or remuneration Evidence should show that the person's salary or other remuneration is significantly high compared with others working in the field. Provide reliable comparative compensation data for the relevant occupation, location, and period, along with pay records or contracts. [6 USCIS-PM F.2(B)(1)]

section: 1. Overview
text: 1. Overview Classification: Immigrant classification for persons of extraordinary ability (EB-1A), under INA 203(b)(1)(A) and 8 CFR 204.5(h). Form: Immigrant Petition for Alien Workers (Form I-140). Who files: A petitioner files on behalf of a noncitizen (the beneficiary). The beneficiary may be the petitioner (self-petition). Job offer: Not required. Anyone may file on the person's behalf, including the person themselves [8 CFR 204.5(h)(5); 8 CFR 204.5(h)(1)]. Evidence: The petitioner must submit evidence showing that the beneficiary is eligible.

text: Sources: INA 203(b)(1)(A)(i)-(iii). Even without a job offer, the person must still show that they intend to continue working in the area of extraordinary ability and that the work will substantially benefit the United States in the future [INA 203(b)(1)(A)(ii)-(iii)]. 2.1 Sustained National or International Acclaim The petitioner must submit evidence that the person has sustained national or international acclaim and that their achievements have been recognized in the field of expertise [INA 203(b)(1)(A)(i); 8 CFR 204.5(h)(3)]. "Sustained" means the acclaim must be maintained. The chapter cites Black's Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019), which defines sustain as to support or maintain, especially over a long period of time. No age limit: "Sustained" does not imply an age limit. A beneficiary may be very young or early in their career and still show sustained acclaim. No fixed time frame: There is no definitive period that counts as "sustained." Comparable level over time: If the person was recognized for a particular achievement, the officer determines whether the person has kept a comparable level of acclaim in the field since that recognition. A person may have achieved acclaim in the past but not maintained a comparable level afterward. 2.2 Continuing to Work in the Area of Expertise The beneficiary must intend to continue working in the area of their expertise [INA 203(b)(1)(A)(ii); 8 CFR 204.5(h)(5)]. # Requirement 1 Has extraordinary ability in the sciences, arts, education, business, or athletics, demonstrated by sustained national or international acclaim, with achievements recognized in the field through extensive documentation. 2 Seeks to enter the United States to continue work in the area of extraordinary ability. 3 Entry will substantially benefit the United States in the future. text: It can be hard to decide whether the intended employment falls within the area of extraordinary ability. Athlete-to-coach scenario: The most problematic cases are those where the acclaim is based on athletic ability but the person intends to work in the U.S. as an athletic coach or manager. Competitive athletics and coaching rely on different sets of skills and are generally not in the same area of expertise. Many extraordinary athletes have nonetheless become extraordinary coaches. General rule: If the beneficiary has clearly achieved recent national or international acclaim as an athlete and has sustained that acclaim in coaching or managing at a national level, officers can consider the totality of the evidence as establishing an overall pattern of sustained acclaim and extraordinary ability. USCIS can then conclude that coaching is within the beneficiary's area of expertise. Extended coaching career: Where the beneficiary has had an extended period, beyond the years of athletic acclaim, to establish a reputation as a coach or manager, officers may place heavier, or exclusive, weight on evidence of achievements as a coach or manager, depending on the facts. 2.3 Entry to Substantially Benefit the United States The person's entry must substantially benefit the United States in the future [INA 203(b)(1)(A)(iii)]. Neither the statute nor the regulations define "substantially benefit." It has been interpreted broadly. Example authority: Matter of Price, 20 I&N Dec. 953 (Assoc. Comm. 1994). A golfer of the beneficiary's caliber would substantially benefit the U.S. prospectively, given the popularity of the sport. The assessment is fact-dependent. There is no standard rule on what substantially benefits the U.S. A Request for Evidence (RFE) may be appropriate if the officer is not yet satisfied that the requirement is met. section: 3. Section B: Evidence of Extraordinary Ability
text: 3. Section B: Evidence of Extraordinary Ability 3.1 General Evidentiary Requirements The regulations describe the types of evidence a petitioner must submit [8 CFR 204.5(h) (3)-(4)]. In general, the petitioner must show: The person has sustained national or international acclaim; and The person's achievements have been recognized in the field of expertise. Initial evidence must include either: 1. Evidence of a one-time achievement (for example, a major internationally recognized award such as the Nobel Prize); or 2. Evidence of at least three of the types of evidence listed in the regulations [8 CFR 204.5(h)(3)]. Other points on evidence: The evidence need not use the word "extraordinary." It should make it readily apparent that the person's contributions to the field qualify. Although the regulatory language sometimes uses plurals, a single piece of evidence in a given category may be enough. Voluminous documentation may still lack sufficient persuasive evidence. The evidence must ultimately establish that the beneficiary "is one of that small percentage who have risen to the very top of the field of endeavor" [8 CFR 204.5(h) (2)]. 3.2 Two-Step Evidentiary Review Officers use a two-step analysis based on Kazarian v. USCIS, 596 F.3d 1115 (9th Cir. 2010). Step Name What the officer does Step 1 Assess whether evidence meets regulatory criteria Determine, by a preponderance of the evidence, which submitted evidence objectively meets the parameters of the regulatory description for that type of evidence. text: Team awards generally qualify where each member receives a trophy, certification or medal; appears on the podium or stage; or is specifically named in the awarding organization's announcement. Examples: members of a musical group who receive an award, and relay team members who appear together on the medal podium. Mere acknowledgment from the recipient does not count as receiving the award from the awarding authority. 2. Is it a lesser nationally or internationally recognized prize or award received for excellence in the field of endeavor? It does not need the recognition and prestige of the Nobel Prize or another award that would qualify as a one-time achievement. Scholastic and limited-eligibility awards: Many scholastic awards lack the requisite recognition, but some may be nationally or internationally recognized as awards for excellence. An award available only to persons within a single locality, employer or school may have little national or international recognition. An award open to members of a well-known national institution (including an R1 or R2 doctoral university) or a professional organization may be nationally recognized. National or international recognition is most often associated with awards to individuals at the highest level of a field. There is no requirement that an award be open to all members of the field, including the most experienced. Limits on competitors are a relevant factor but not conclusive. An award may still be nationally or internationally recognized if limited to youth, amateurs or early-career professionals. Example: awards to new players or "rookies" in major sports leagues may receive national or international media coverage. Definition (footnote): The Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education designates R1 and R2 doctoral universities as having very high or high research activity, respectively. The designation is based on public federal data on doctoral degrees awarded and total research expenditures.

section: USCIS Policy Manual, Volume 6, Part F, Chapter 2
text: Officer determination: Does the association, in which the person claims present or past membership, require outstanding achievements in the field as judged by recognized experts in that field? Key considerations: The petitioner must show that membership requires outstanding achievements in the relevant field, as judged by recognized national or international experts. Associations may have multiple membership levels. The level held must show that recognized national or international experts judged the person to have attained outstanding achievements in the field. Example from the chapter (engineering): General membership in an international organization for engineering and technology professionals may not meet the criterion. The organization's fellow level may qualify if it requires, in part, accomplishments that contributed importantly to the advancement or application of engineering, science and technology, and a council of experts and a committee of current fellows judges the nominations. Example from the chapter (AI): Fellow membership in a scientific society dedicated to artificial intelligence may qualify if it is based on recognition of significant, sustained contributions to the field and a panel of current fellows selects new fellows. The chapter lists factors indicating membership was not based on outstanding achievement. These apply where membership rested solely on certain factors, alone or in aggregate. The specific list was not captured in the retrieved text. Current membership is not required. Past membership may qualify [8 CFR 204.5(h)(3) (ii)]. However, if there is no recent evidence, the time elapsed since membership may be considered in the final merits determination as bearing on whether acclaim has been sustained.

text: 2. Does the publication qualify as a professional publication, major trade publication or major media? Key considerations: The material should be about the person and their work, not only about the employer or another organization. Marketing material created to sell the person's products or promote their services is generally not published material about the person. This includes seemingly objective content in major print publications that the person or employer paid for. The person need not be the only subject. Material on a broader topic that includes substantial discussion of the person's work and mentions the person in connection with it may qualify. Material focused mainly on work by a team the person belongs to may be considered if it mentions the person in connection with the work, or if other record evidence documents the person's significant role. Forms of evidence include print or online newspaper or magazine articles, popular or academic journal articles, books, textbooks, similar publications, and transcripts of professional or major audio or video coverage. Factors for judging the publication: intended audience (for professional and major trade publications) and relative circulation, readership or viewership (for major trade publications and other major media).

text: Criterion 4: Judging the Work of Others Regulation: 8 CFR 204.5(h)(3)(iv). Participation, individually or on a panel, as a judge of the work of others in the same or an allied field of specification for which classification is sought. Officer determination: Has the person acted as a judge of the work of others in the same or an allied field of specialization? Key consideration: The petitioner must show that the person was invited to judge and actually participated in judging. Example: a peer review might be documented with a journal's request to review plus evidence the person completed the review.

section: USCIS Policy Manual, Volume 6, Part F, Chapter 2
text: Officer determinations: 1. Has the person made original contributions in the field? 2. Are those contributions of major significance to the field? Key considerations: The focus is whether the original work constitutes major, significant contributions. Evidence that the work was funded, patented or published may show originality but does not by itself establish major significance. Probative evidence examples: Published research that provoked widespread commentary on its importance from others in the field. Documentation that the work is highly cited relative to others' work in the field. A patented technology that attracted significant attention or commercialization. Pending patents: USCIS generally requires additional supporting evidence of originality, such as detailed reference letters. Expert letters can give valuable context, especially when the record has documentation corroborating the claimed significance. Letters should specifically describe the contribution and its significance, and should state the basis of the writer's knowledge and expertise.

section: Criterion 6: Authorship of Scholarly Articles
text: Criterion 6: Authorship of Scholarly Articles Regulation: 8 CFR 204.5(h)(3)(vi). Authorship of scholarly articles in the field, in professional or major trade publications or other major media. Officer determinations: 1. Has the person authored scholarly articles in the field? 2. Does the publication qualify as a professional publication, major trade publication or major media? What is a scholarly article? It reports on original research, experimentation or philosophical discourse. It is written by a researcher or expert, often affiliated with a college, university or research institution. It is generally peer reviewed by other experts in the field of specialization. text: It should generally have footnotes, endnotes or a bibliography, and may include graphs, charts, videos or pictures. Other fields: A scholarly article should be written for learned persons in the field. "Learned" means having profound knowledge gained by study (Oxford English Dictionary). Learned persons include all persons having profound knowledge of a field. Conference proceedings: Many conference presentations are not published. section: Criterion 7: Display at Artistic Exhibitions or Showcases
text: Criterion 7: Display at Artistic Exhibitions or Showcases Regulation: 8 CFR 204.5(h)(3)(vii). Display of the person's work in the field at artistic exhibitions or showcases. Officer determinations: 1. Is the displayed work the person's own work product? 2. Were the venues (virtual or otherwise) artistic exhibitions or showcases? Key points: Merriam-Webster defines "exhibition" as a public showing (of works of art, objects of manufacture or athletic skill). The regulation says "artistic," so the exhibition or showcase must be artistic in nature. Non-artistic exhibitions or showcases are considered only as part of a properly supported comparable evidence claim.

text: Leading vs. critical role: Leading role: The evidence shows the person is or was a leader within the organization, division or department. A title with matching duties can help. Critical role: The person contributed in a way of significant importance to the outcome of the organization's activities (or those of a division or department). A supporting role may be critical if the person's performance in it is or was important. It is the person's performance, not the title, that determines whether a role is critical. Letters from persons with personal knowledge can be especially helpful here, if they contain detailed, probative information on how the role was leading or critical. Evidence of experience must consist of letters from employers [8 CFR 204.5(g)(1)]. Distinguished reputation: Size or longevity alone is not determinative. It is considered with other information. Other relevant factors include the scale of the customer base and relevant media coverage. Academic departments, programs and institutions: Officers may consider relevant, credible national rankings and receipt of government research grants as positive factors. Startups: Officers may consider significant funding from government entities, venture capital funds, angel investors or similar funders, commensurate with funding rounds generally achieved for that startup's stage and industry, as a positive factor. Merriam-Webster defines "distinguished" as "marked by eminence, distinction, or excellence" or "befitting an eminent person."

section: Criterion 10: Commercial Successes in the Performing Arts
text: Criterion 10: Commercial Successes in the Performing Arts Regulation: 8 CFR 204.5(h)(3)(x). Commercial successes in the performing arts, shown by box office receipts or record, cassette, compact disk or video sales. Officer determination: Has the person enjoyed commercial successes in the performing arts? Key points: The focus is volume of sales and box office receipts as a measure of commercial success. Merely recording and releasing music, or performing in theatrical, motion picture or television productions, is not enough on its own. The evidence must show that sales volume and box office receipts reflect the person's commercial success relative to others in similar pursuits in the performing arts.

text: Officers must consider (a) whether the regulatory criteria are readily applicable to the person's occupation and, if not, (b) whether the evidence is truly comparable to the listed criteria. A general, unsupported assertion that a criterion does not readily apply is not probative. General claims that USCIS should accept witness letters as comparable evidence are not persuasive. A detailed, specific and credible statement from the petitioner can be enough to establish that a criterion is not readily applicable.

section: Comparable evidence is not considered where a criterion is readily applicable to the
text: Comparable evidence is not considered where a criterion is readily applicable to the occupation. A criterion need not be entirely inapplicable. It is enough if the petitioner shows it is not easily applicable to the person's job or profession. "Readily" means "easily" or "without much difficulty." "Occupation" means "the principal business of one's life" (Merriam-Webster).

section: Comparable evidence may be considered for STEM fields, as with all extraordinary
text: Comparable evidence may be considered for STEM fields, as with all extraordinary ability petitions. Examples from the chapter: If publishing scholarly articles is not readily applicable to someone in industry rather than academia, presenting work at a major trade show may be of comparable significance. If a high salary is not readily applicable to an entrepreneur, highly valued equity holdings in the startup may be of comparable significance. There is no comparable evidence for the one-time achievement of a major, internationally recognized award. Limits of Step 1 The evidence reviewed in Step 1 is reviewed again in Step 2. Meeting the regulatory criteria in Step 1 does not by itself establish eligibility [INA 203(b)(1)(A)]. Example, judging: Participating in judging the work of others in the same or an allied field should satisfy the Step 1 criterion regardless of circumstances. Step 2 then evaluates whether the participation shows the person is one of that small percentage at the very top and enjoys sustained acclaim. section: 5. Step 2: Final Merits Determination
text: 5. Step 2: Final Merits Determination Standard: Preponderance of the evidence. Question: Considering the petition in its entirety, has the person shown sustained national or international acclaim, with achievements recognized in the field, indicating they are one of that small percentage who has risen to the very top of the field of endeavor? Rules for officers: Officers may not limit the kind of evidence they think the person should be able to submit, and deny because a particular type is absent, if the person submitted other evidence that meets the regulatory requirements. Example: an officer may think an extraordinary person should have published articles about them. The officer cannot deny solely because none were submitted, as long as other evidence meets three qualifying criteria and shows the person is extraordinary. Decisions rest on the type and quality of evidence submitted, not assumptions about unaddressed criteria. In Step 2 officers consider any potentially relevant evidence in the record, even if it does not fit a regulatory criterion or was not presented as comparable evidence. All evidence is weighed in its totality. Some evidence weighs more favorably alone, and some is more persuasive in combination. Examples of evidence that may help officers assess quality and standing (non- exhaustive): 1. Highly ranked journals: Articles (including published conference proceedings) in journals that are highly ranked relative to others in the field, shown for example by impact factor. Prestige may be greater if the person is the most significant contributor, a senior author or the sole author. Impact factor: a measure of a journal's influence. Example: an h-index of 10 means 10 publications with 10 or more citations each, but not 11 publications with at least 11 citations (Hirsch, PNAS 2005). Balance of evidence: A person may be stronger in one evidentiary area than others, but the totality of the evidence must establish that the person is extraordinary. Officer duties when denying or requesting evidence: Do not make merely general assertions about failure to show eligibility. Articulate specific reasons why the petitioner did not show extraordinary ability by a preponderance of the evidence [INA 203(b)(1)(A)]. If the officer believes the stated facts are not true and can explain why, the officer denies and explains in a written denial. When requesting additional evidence, explain the deficiencies in the evidence already submitted and, if possible, give examples of persuasive evidence the petitioner might provide. Merely restating the requirements or saying the evidence is insufficient does not help the petitioner overcome the deficiencies.

section: 6. Other Evidentiary Considerations
text: 6. Other Evidentiary Considerations 6.1 Letters of Support Letters carry weight but should not form the cornerstone of a successful claim. Statements by witnesses should be corroborated by documentary evidence in the record. Letters should explain in specific terms why the witnesses believe the beneficiary is of extraordinary caliber. Letters that merely repeat USCIS definitions or make general, expansive statements are generally not persuasive. Relationship or affiliation between the beneficiary and the witness is a factor in evaluating the statement's significance. It is generally expected that someone with sustained national or international acclaim has been recognized well beyond their personal and professional acquaintances. Letters from others in the field that only make general assertions may show at most that the beneficiary is a competent, respected figure in the field. They are considered but do not necessarily show extraordinary ability. USCIS Policy Manual, Volume 6, Part F, Chapter 2: Extraordinary Ability (EB-1A) Page 16 of 20

text: 6.2 Immigrant Petitions Filed for Former O-1 Nonimmigrants A prior O-1 approval (extraordinary ability, or extraordinary achievement for the motion picture and television industry) is relevant and can indicate eligibility but is not determinative. Each petition is separate and independent and is adjudicated on its own merits under its own statutory and regulatory provisions. The O-1 classification has different standards for the arts and for motion picture and television. Example: a person in the arts may have "distinction" for O-1 purposes yet not meet the immigrant standard of being among the small percentage at the very top of the field. Some courts have asked USCIS to explain why a person previously classified in a roughly analogous nonimmigrant category is not eligible for the immigrant classification. Where possible, officers issuing denials in such cases should briefly explain why the petitioner failed to meet its burden despite the earlier O-1 approval.
